_comment: The Word choice notes' quotations (crates/atlas-cli/src/extra_grammar.rs reads this file; it has no kind, so the Layers build passes over it).

Where each quotation in config/grammar.json was read. work and page are the term's own; quote is the words as config/grammar.json gives them; found_in is the address of the scan's text for that page; page_address opens the page itself; context is the scan's text around the quotation, as it was copied that day; read is the date; note says anything the reader should know, above all where the scan's text differs from what is given.

robertson-short: A. T. Robertson, A Short Grammar of the Greek New Testament, for Students Familiar with the Elements of Greek, third edition (New York: Hodder and Stoughton, George H. Doran Company; "Copyright, 1908, by A. T. Robertson"), the archive.org scan shortgrammarofgr00robeuoft, which archive.org dates [1912] and marks NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT. The printed page is the scan's leaf number less 40, by the scan's own page-number file.

How these were read on 2026-11-14: from the scan's text layer (its OCR), one page at a time, in two separate readings on the same day, the second copying each sentence and the two sentences either side of it word by word. Both readings agree on every quotation. No page image was seen, so each quotation is the scan's text, not a proof-read of the print: where that text is plainly a misreading ("asa" for "as a", "haye" for "have", a word broken at a line end), the note says so and gives what the context was changed to.

green-grammar: William Henry Green, A Grammar of the Hebrew Language, second edition, with corrections and copious indexes (New York: John Wiley, 1861), the archive.org scan grammarofhebrew00gree. The printed page is the scan's leaf number less 16, by the scan's own page-number file. Read on 2026-11-14 from the scan's text layer, each quotation at least twice in this scan (a note says where a word rests on the other scan), and once more in the scan of the third edition of 1863 (grammarofhebrew1863gree), which has the same page and section numbers on the pages compared and gives the same words. No page image was seen. Green's names are older than the tags': his preterite is the perfect, his future the imperfect, Vav Conversive the "and" of the consecutive forms, Kal the simple pattern. In these records the context is the words just before the quotation, the quotation and the words just after, pieced from short copies of the scan's text; Hebrew letters in it are garbled and kept as read.

checked.quote: the present tense expresses incompleted action
checked.context: The present is the normal tense for incompletion in all the modes. The stem of the imperfect is the same as that of the present. (a) The present. So, then, the present tense expresses incompleted action, which action in any given case may be momentary, prolonged, simultaneous, descriptive, repeated, customary, attempted, interrupted, or begun, according to the nature of the case or the meaning of the verb itself. In vivid narration past or future incompleted action can be conceived of and stated in the present indicative. This is not a peculiarity of language at all.
checked.note: A clause: the sentence opens "So, then," and goes on after "action,". The context runs from the foot of page 139 over the heading "(a) The present." The scan's text has "attempted. interrupted," where the list otherwise uses commas; a comma is given here.

checked.quote: Too much has been read into the Greek tenses and not enough allowance is always made for the meaning of the verb itself.
checked.context: (b) The imperfect. The imperfect likewise expresses incompleted action which in any given case may be either momentary, simultaneous, prolonged, descriptive, repeated, customary, interrupted, attempted, or begun, according to the context or the meaning of the verb. Too much has been read into the Greek tenses and not enough allowance is always made for the meaning of the verb itself. To wink the eye, for instance, is obviously different as to length of duration from eating one’s dinner and living a life. With due regard to this point and the context the Greek imperfect will be found always true to its root idea.
checked.note: The second sentence of the section "(b) The imperfect."

checked.context: With due regard to this point and the context the Greek imperfect will be found always true to its root idea. The participle with e«iué is very common in the New Testament, especially in Luke. The imperfect is the descriptive tense of narrative and varies the simple monotony of the aorist. It puts life into the story like the present. Some imperfects that are very common like éAeyey perhaps do not differ in stem from an old second aorist (cf. &AaBev).

If the action is not to be described as completed or incompleted, put it in the aorist. General statements or illustrations are often put in the aorist and you are left to draw the inference. This is really * a representative aorist..

checked.quote: the aorist represents the action as a point
checked.context: See the exact force of the Greek aorist in every instance. That force is well represented by Moulton (Prolegomena, p. 109) as punctiliar or point action. The thing to bear in mind is that the aorist represents the action as a point. In itself it may have continued a long time. It is precisely the idea of the aorist (undefined action) that it does not distinguish between complete or incomplete action. It may be used of either.

checked.quote: When therefore the past perfect is used, the completion in past time is distinctly emphasized.
checked.context: In the indicative, future time was almost wholly indicated by one tense, present time by two tenses, past time by three though the aorist and the imperfect held the field against the past perfect. The aorist was used of past time in the indicative, as a matter of course, unless there was a special desire to lay stress on the incompletion or the completion of the action. When therefore the past perfect is used, the completion in past time is distinctly emphasized. But as a rule the Greeks did not care to work out the relation of time so carefully. The simple aorist told the story consecutively and one could see the rest for himself.
checked.note: Robertson calls the pluperfect the past perfect. checked.quote: The Greek verb itself contains the personal subject
